about: Principles of Medicine (MEDI40001) is the opening core module of Imperial's MBBS/BSc, worth 10 credits and taught in the autumn term of Year 1, according to the 2026-27 programme specification. It lays the scientific groundwork for the body-systems teaching that follows; an unofficial students' union page (last updated in 2022, so possibly out of date) describes it as covering cell biology and metabolism, haematology, immunology and genetics through lectures, tutorials, lab practicals and reading sessions. No official topic-by-topic syllabus is published, so the topics here are grouped under those unofficial headings. The programme specification says Phase 1 knowledge is assessed with single best answer, very short answer and/or short answer questions, and that students must pass each module; check your module handbook for this module's exact assessment.
topics: Energy metabolism: glycolysis, the TCA cycle and oxidative phosphorylation
Metabolic integration: fed and fasting states
Adaptive immunity: B cells, T cells and antibodies
Genetics: DNA, gene expression and inheritance

notes.body:
Almost every later topic in medicine assumes you know what the parts of a cell do and how substances cross membranes. This is the base layer of Principles of Medicine.

Organelles and their jobs
- Nucleus: holds the DNA; transcription and RNA processing happen here. The nucleolus makes ribosomal RNA.
- Rough endoplasmic reticulum (RER): ribosome-studded; makes proteins destined for secretion, for membranes or for lysosomes. Plasma cells and pancreatic acinar cells are packed with RER.
- Smooth ER: lipid and steroid synthesis, detoxification (abundant in hepatocytes), and calcium storage (in muscle it is the sarcoplasmic reticulum).
- Golgi apparatus: modifies (e.g. glycosylation), sorts and packages proteins into vesicles.
- Lysosomes: acidic compartments (pH roughly 4.5–5) containing hydrolytic enzymes that break down engulfed or worn-out material. Inherited lysosomal enzyme deficiencies cause storage disorders.
- Peroxisomes: oxidise very-long-chain fatty acids and use catalase to break down hydrogen peroxide.
- Mitochondria: site of the TCA cycle and oxidative phosphorylation; they have their own circular DNA, inherited through the mother.
- Cytoskeleton: actin microfilaments (shape, movement), intermediate filaments (mechanical strength, e.g. keratins) and microtubules (tubulin; mitotic spindle, intracellular transport, cilia).

The plasma membrane
The membrane is a phospholipid bilayer with embedded and attached proteins, described by the fluid mosaic model (Singer and Nicolson, 1972). Hydrophobic tails face inwards, so the core is a barrier to ions and large polar molecules. Cholesterol buffers fluidity. Integral proteins act as channels, carriers, pumps and receptors; carbohydrate chains on the outer surface form the glycocalyx and take part in cell recognition (the ABO antigens are an example).

How things cross membranes
- Simple diffusion: down a concentration gradient, no protein needed. Works for small non-polar molecules such as O₂, CO₂ and steroid hormones. Fick's law: rate is proportional to surface area × concentration difference ÷ membrane thickness. This is why lung disease that thickens the alveolar wall impairs gas exchange.
- Facilitated diffusion: down a gradient through a channel or carrier (e.g. GLUT transporters for glucose). Carrier-mediated transport is specific and saturable.
- Primary active transport: uses ATP directly. The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase moves 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in per ATP; it keeps intracellular Na⁺ low and K⁺ high and is electrogenic. Cardiac glycosides such as digoxin inhibit this pump.
- Secondary active transport: uses the Na⁺ gradient made by the pump. Symport example: SGLT1 in the small intestine carries Na⁺ and glucose in together. Antiport example: the Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger.
- Vesicular transport: endocytosis (including receptor-mediated uptake of LDL) and exocytosis (e.g. neurotransmitter release).

Osmosis and tonicity
Water moves towards the side with the higher concentration of osmotically active particles. Worked example: 0.9% sodium chloride is 9 g/L; dividing by the molar mass (58.44 g/mol) gives about 154 mmol/L, and because NaCl dissociates into two ions the theoretical osmolarity is about 308 mOsm/L. Because the ions do not behave ideally, its effective osmolality is lower (roughly 285 mOsm/kg), close to that of plasma (approximately 275–295 mOsm/kg), so "normal saline" is roughly isotonic. Red cells placed in a hypotonic solution swell and may lyse; in a hypertonic solution they shrink (crenate).

Clinical links
- Cystic fibrosis: faulty CFTR, a chloride channel, gives thick secretions in lungs and pancreas.
- Oral rehydration solution works because glucose-coupled sodium uptake via SGLT1 still functions in many diarrhoeal illnesses, and water follows the absorbed solute.

Exam tips: be precise about which transport type uses ATP directly and which uses an ion gradient, give the 3 Na⁺ : 2 K⁺ ratio, and show your working (molarity × number of particles) in osmolarity questions.

Proteins do most of the work in cells, and enzymes are the proteins most often examined. Expect questions on structure, Michaelis–Menten kinetics and inhibition.

Protein structure
- Primary: the amino acid sequence, joined by peptide bonds.
- Secondary: local folding held by hydrogen bonds in the backbone (α-helix, β-pleated sheet).
- Tertiary: the overall 3D fold of one chain, stabilised by hydrophobic interactions, ionic bonds, hydrogen bonds and disulfide bridges.
- Quaternary: assembly of several chains; adult haemoglobin (HbA) is α₂β₂.
Heat, extreme pH and some chemicals denature proteins by disrupting the higher levels of structure; the primary sequence is unchanged.

How enzymes work
Enzymes are biological catalysts. They lower the activation energy of a reaction, speeding up the approach to equilibrium, but they do not change the equilibrium position or the overall free-energy change (ΔG). Substrates bind at the active site; the induced-fit model (Koshland, 1958) describes the enzyme changing shape as substrate binds. Many enzymes need cofactors (metal ions) or coenzymes derived from vitamins: NAD⁺ from niacin, FAD from riboflavin, thiamine pyrophosphate from thiamine.

Michaelis–Menten kinetics
v = Vmax[S] / (Km + [S])
- Vmax: the maximum rate when the enzyme is saturated.
- Km: the substrate concentration giving half Vmax. A low Km means the enzyme reaches half-maximal rate at a low substrate concentration (often described as high apparent affinity).
Worked example: Vmax = 100 units, Km = 2 mM. At [S] = 2 mM, v = 100 × 2 / 4 = 50 (half Vmax, as the definition requires). At [S] = 6 mM, v = 600 / 8 = 75. At [S] = 18 mM, v = 1800 / 20 = 90: the curve flattens as the enzyme saturates.
The Lineweaver–Burk (double-reciprocal) plot rearranges this to 1/v = (Km/Vmax)(1/[S]) + 1/Vmax: the y-intercept is 1/Vmax and the x-intercept is −1/Km.

Inhibition
- Competitive: inhibitor competes for the active site. Apparent Km rises, Vmax is unchanged, and high substrate overcomes it. Example: methotrexate competing with folate at dihydrofolate reductase. With Km doubled to 4 mM in the example above, v at 2 mM falls from 50 to about 33.
- Non-competitive: inhibitor binds elsewhere; Vmax falls, Km unchanged; extra substrate cannot overcome it.
- Uncompetitive: binds only the enzyme–substrate complex; both Vmax and apparent Km fall.
- Irreversible: covalent modification. Aspirin irreversibly acetylates cyclo-oxygenase, which is why its antiplatelet effect lasts for the life of the platelet.

Regulation
- Allosteric enzymes give sigmoidal rather than hyperbolic curves and respond to effectors at separate sites (phosphofructokinase-1 is the classic metabolic example).
- Covalent modification, especially phosphorylation by kinases and removal by phosphatases.
- Zymogens: inactive precursors activated by cleavage, e.g. trypsinogen to trypsin by enteropeptidase in the duodenum. Premature activation in the pancreas contributes to pancreatitis.
- Isoenzymes: different forms catalysing the same reaction. Hexokinase (most tissues) has a low Km and is inhibited by its product glucose-6-phosphate; glucokinase (liver and pancreatic β cells) has a much higher Km and is not inhibited by glucose-6-phosphate, so it works as a glucose sensor after meals.

Clinical relevance
Enzymes leaking from damaged cells are used as blood markers, for example ALT for hepatocyte injury and creatine kinase for muscle damage. Many drugs are enzyme inhibitors (statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase; ACE inhibitors block angiotensin-converting enzyme).

Exam tips: always state what happens to Vmax and Km for each inhibitor type, and check any calculation by confirming that v = Vmax/2 when [S] = Km.

notes.h: Glycolysis, the TCA cycle and oxidative phosphorylation
notes.body:
Cells turn the chemical energy in fuel into ATP. You need the location, inputs, outputs and control points of each stage, and an ATP tally you can justify.

Glycolysis (cytosol)
- Glucose (6C) is split into 2 pyruvate (3C).
- Net yield per glucose: 2 ATP and 2 NADH (4 ATP are made but 2 are spent in the early steps).
- Three essentially irreversible, regulated steps: hexokinase/glucokinase, phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1) and pyruvate kinase. PFK-1 is the main control point: activated by AMP and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate, inhibited by ATP and citrate.
- No oxygen needed. Without oxygen (or without mitochondria), pyruvate is reduced to lactate by lactate dehydrogenase, which regenerates NAD⁺ so glycolysis can continue. Red blood cells have no mitochondria and depend entirely on glycolysis.

Link reaction (mitochondrial matrix)
The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex converts pyruvate to acetyl-CoA, releasing CO₂ and making NADH. It needs thiamine (as thiamine pyrophosphate). The reaction is irreversible, which is why fatty acids (broken down to acetyl-CoA) cannot be used for net glucose synthesis.

TCA (Krebs) cycle (matrix)
Acetyl-CoA (2C) joins oxaloacetate (4C) to make citrate (6C). Per turn of the cycle:
- 3 NADH, 1 FADH₂, 1 GTP (or ATP) and 2 CO₂.
- Each glucose gives two acetyl-CoA, so two turns.
The cycle is amphibolic: its intermediates also feed biosynthesis (e.g. haem from succinyl-CoA, amino acids).

Electron transport chain and oxidative phosphorylation (inner mitochondrial membrane)
- NADH donates electrons at complex I; FADH₂ (from succinate dehydrogenase, which is complex II) enters via complex II.
- Electrons pass through ubiquinone, complex III, cytochrome c and complex IV, where oxygen is the final acceptor and is reduced to water.
- Complexes I, III and IV pump protons into the intermembrane space. ATP synthase lets them flow back and uses this proton-motive force to make ATP. This is Mitchell's chemiosmotic theory (proposed 1961).
- Approximate yields: about 2.5 ATP per NADH and 1.5 ATP per FADH₂.

ATP tally per glucose (modern estimate)
- NADH: 2 (glycolysis) + 2 (link) + 6 (TCA) = 10, × 2.5 = 25
- FADH₂: 2 × 1.5 = 3
- ATP/GTP made directly: 2 (glycolysis) + 2 (TCA) = 4
- Total about 32. If cytosolic NADH enters by the glycerol-phosphate shuttle (worth about 1.5 each) the total is about 30. Older textbooks quote 36–38 using whole-number P/O ratios; current teaching uses roughly 30–32.

Inhibitors and uncouplers
- Cyanide and carbon monoxide inhibit complex IV, stopping aerobic ATP production.
- Uncouplers let protons leak back without passing through ATP synthase, so energy is released as heat. 2,4-dinitrophenol is a toxic example; uncoupling protein 1 (thermogenin) in brown fat does this physiologically for heat production in newborns.

Other fuels
Fatty acids are carried into mitochondria by the carnitine shuttle and broken down by β-oxidation into acetyl-CoA, NADH and FADH₂, which feed the TCA cycle and chain. Fat gives more ATP per gram than carbohydrate.

Exam tips: state where each stage occurs, the products per glucose (remember two turns of the TCA cycle) and why lactate forms when oxygen or mitochondria are lacking. If you give an ATP total, show the assumptions behind it.

notes.h: Metabolic integration: fed and fasting states
notes.body:
Different tissues share the work of keeping blood glucose and fuel supply steady. Insulin and glucagon drive the switch between storing fuel after meals and releasing it during fasting.

Insulin: the fed state
Release from pancreatic β cells: glucose enters through GLUT2 and is phosphorylated by glucokinase; metabolism raises ATP, which closes ATP-sensitive K⁺ channels; the cell depolarises, voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels open and Ca²⁺ influx triggers exocytosis of insulin. (Sulfonylureas act by closing the same K⁺ channels.)
Actions (anabolic):
- Moves GLUT4 transporters to the surface of skeletal muscle and adipose cells, increasing glucose uptake.
- Liver and muscle: stimulates glycogen synthesis.
- Liver and adipose: stimulates fatty acid and triglyceride synthesis; inhibits lipolysis.
- Inhibits hepatic gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis.
- Promotes protein synthesis and cellular K⁺ uptake.

Glucagon: the fasting state
Released from α cells when glucose falls. It acts mainly on the liver: stimulates glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis, and promotes fatty acid oxidation and ketone body formation. Muscle glycogen cannot supply blood glucose directly because muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase; it is used locally. Other counter-regulatory hormones are adrenaline, cortisol and growth hormone.

The fasting timeline
- After a meal: insulin dominates; fuel is stored.
- Early fast (hours): hepatic glycogenolysis maintains blood glucose. Liver glycogen is largely used up within about a day.
- Ongoing fast: gluconeogenesis in the liver (and to a lesser extent the kidney) from lactate (Cori cycle), alanine (glucose–alanine cycle) and glycerol from triglyceride breakdown. Fatty acids released from adipose tissue fuel muscle and liver.
- Prolonged starvation: the liver makes ketone bodies (acetoacetate and β-hydroxybutyrate) from acetyl-CoA. The brain adapts to use ketones for a large share of its energy, which reduces the need to break down muscle protein for gluconeogenesis.
- Fixed demands: red cells need glucose throughout (no mitochondria), and the brain cannot use fatty acids directly.

Key principle: even-chain fatty acids cannot make net glucose, because acetyl-CoA cannot be converted back to pyruvate. The glycerol backbone of triglyceride can.

Clinical relevance: diabetes mellitus
- Type 1: autoimmune destruction of β cells gives absolute insulin deficiency. Uncontrolled lipolysis and ketogenesis can lead to diabetic ketoacidosis.
- Type 2: insulin resistance together with progressive β-cell dysfunction; strongly associated with excess adiposity and inactivity. Lifestyle change is central to prevention and management.
- Diagnosis in the UK commonly uses HbA1c of 48 mmol/mol (6.5%) or more, or a fasting plasma glucose of 7.0 mmol/L or more, with confirmation required in people without symptoms. HbA1c reflects average glycaemia over roughly the previous 2–3 months because red cells live about 120 days; it is unreliable when red cell turnover is abnormal (e.g. haemolysis, some haemoglobinopathies).
- Hypoglycaemia activates the sympathetic nervous system and adrenal medulla, giving autonomic symptoms (tremor and palpitations from adrenaline; sweating and hunger largely via sympathetic cholinergic and other pathways), usually before neuroglycopenic symptoms such as confusion. People with long-standing diabetes can lose these warning symptoms (impaired awareness of hypoglycaemia).

Exam tips: organise answers by tissue (liver, muscle, adipose, brain) and by time (fed, early fast, prolonged fast). Explaining why fat cannot become glucose, and why the liver rather than muscle exports glucose, earns marks.

Haematology in the first year covers how blood cells are made, how haemoglobin carries oxygen and how anaemia is classified.

Haematopoiesis
In adults, blood cells are made in the bone marrow (mainly axial skeleton and proximal long bones) from haematopoietic stem cells. These give rise to a myeloid line (red cells, platelets, granulocytes, monocytes) and a lymphoid line (B, T and NK cells). Red cell production is driven by erythropoietin, made mainly by peritubular interstitial cells in the kidney in response to low oxygen delivery; this is why chronic kidney disease causes anaemia.

Red cells
Biconcave discs without a nucleus or mitochondria, giving a large surface area and flexibility to squeeze through capillaries. They live about 120 days and are removed by macrophages, mainly in the spleen. Haem is broken down to bilirubin; iron is recycled.

Haemoglobin and oxygen carriage
- Adult haemoglobin (HbA) is α₂β₂; fetal haemoglobin (HbF) is α₂γ₂.
- Each of the four haem groups contains ferrous iron (Fe²⁺) and binds one O₂, so each Hb molecule carries up to four O₂.
- Binding is cooperative: once one O₂ binds, the others bind more easily. This gives the sigmoid oxygen dissociation curve. The P50 (PO₂ at 50% saturation) is approximately 3.5 kPa (about 26–27 mmHg) for adult blood.
- Right shift (lower affinity, more O₂ unloading in tissues): raised CO₂, raised H⁺ (the Bohr effect), raised temperature and raised 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate. Exercising muscle creates exactly these conditions.
- Left shift (higher affinity): HbF (binds 2,3-BPG poorly, helping the fetus take O₂ from maternal blood), alkalosis, cold and carbon monoxide. CO binds haem with roughly 200–250 times the affinity of O₂ and also stops the remaining sites from releasing O₂.

Anaemia
Anaemia is a haemoglobin concentration below the reference range for age and sex. It is a finding, not a diagnosis; the mean cell volume (MCV, normally about 80–100 fL) is used to narrow the cause.
- Microcytic (low MCV): iron deficiency (commonest cause worldwide), thalassaemia trait, anaemia of chronic disease (sometimes).
- Normocytic: acute blood loss, anaemia of chronic disease, chronic kidney disease, haemolysis.
- Macrocytic (high MCV): vitamin B12 or folate deficiency (megaloblastic), alcohol excess, liver disease, hypothyroidism, a high reticulocyte count.

Iron and B12 handling
- Iron is absorbed in the duodenum as Fe²⁺ through DMT1 and leaves enterocytes through ferroportin. Hepcidin, made by the liver, blocks ferroportin; inflammation raises hepcidin, trapping iron in stores (part of anaemia of chronic disease).
- Ferritin reflects iron stores: low ferritin indicates iron deficiency. Ferritin is also an acute-phase protein, so a normal level does not exclude iron deficiency during inflammation.
- B12 needs intrinsic factor from gastric parietal cells and is absorbed in the terminal ileum. Pernicious anaemia is autoimmune loss of intrinsic factor or parietal cells; ileal resection or Crohn's disease can also cause deficiency.
- Common symptoms of anaemia: fatigue, breathlessness on exertion, palpitations; signs include pallor and, if severe, tachycardia and a flow murmur.

White cells and platelets
Neutrophils are the most numerous white cells in adult blood and are first responders in bacterial infection. Lymphocytes mediate adaptive immunity; monocytes become tissue macrophages; eosinophils rise in parasitic infection and allergy; basophils release histamine. Platelets are fragments of megakaryocytes and survive about 7–10 days.

Exam tips: in data questions, classify the anaemia by MCV first, then use ferritin, B12/folate and reticulocyte count to reason towards a cause. Be ready to draw and explain shifts of the dissociation curve.

Haemostasis stops bleeding while keeping blood fluid elsewhere. Too little causes bleeding disorders; too much causes thrombosis.

Primary haemostasis (the platelet plug)
- Injury exposes subendothelial collagen; the vessel constricts briefly.
- Adhesion: von Willebrand factor (vWF) bridges collagen to platelet glycoprotein Ib.
- Activation: platelets change shape and release ADP and thromboxane A₂, recruiting more platelets.
- Aggregation: activated glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptors bind fibrinogen, linking platelets together.
Aspirin works here by irreversibly blocking cyclo-oxygenase and so thromboxane A₂ production.

Secondary haemostasis (coagulation)
The classical cascade is still useful for interpreting tests:
- Extrinsic pathway: tissue factor + factor VIIa. In the body this is the main trigger of coagulation.
- Intrinsic pathway: factors XII, XI, IX and VIII.
- Common pathway: factor X → Xa, which with Va converts prothrombin (II) to thrombin (IIa). Thrombin converts fibrinogen to fibrin, and factor XIIIa cross-links fibrin to stabilise the clot. Thrombin also amplifies the process by activating V, VIII, XI and platelets.
The modern cell-based model describes initiation (tissue factor-bearing cells), amplification and propagation on the activated platelet surface; it explains why haemophilia causes bleeding even though the extrinsic pathway is intact.

Laboratory tests
- Prothrombin time (PT, reported as INR): extrinsic + common pathways; prolonged by warfarin and liver disease.
- Activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT): intrinsic + common; prolonged in haemophilia A and B.
Vitamin K is needed for the γ-carboxylation of factors II, VII, IX and X and of proteins C and S. Warfarin blocks vitamin K epoxide reductase, reducing functional levels of these factors.

Natural anticoagulants and fibrinolysis
- Antithrombin inactivates thrombin and Xa; heparin works by greatly enhancing antithrombin.
- Protein C, activated with protein S as cofactor, inactivates Va and VIIIa. Factor V Leiden resists this inactivation and is a common inherited thrombophilia in people of European ancestry.
- Tissue factor pathway inhibitor limits the extrinsic pathway.
- Fibrinolysis: tissue plasminogen activator converts plasminogen to plasmin, which breaks down fibrin. D-dimer is a breakdown product of cross-linked fibrin.

Thrombosis
Virchow's triad: stasis of blood flow, endothelial injury and hypercoagulability. Example: a long-haul flight (stasis) after surgery (hypercoagulable state) raises the risk of deep vein thrombosis.

Bleeding disorders
- Haemophilia A (factor VIII) and B (factor IX): X-linked recessive, so mostly affecting males; joint and muscle bleeds.
- von Willebrand disease: the commonest inherited bleeding disorder, usually autosomal dominant; mucosal bleeding such as nosebleeds and heavy periods.

Blood groups
- ABO: red cells carry A, B, both or neither antigen. People make naturally occurring antibodies (mostly IgM) against the antigens they lack, so group O plasma contains anti-A and anti-B.
- Group O red cells lack A and B antigens, so they are used as "universal" red cells in emergencies; group AB patients have neither antibody and can receive red cells of any ABO group. For plasma the logic reverses: AB plasma has no anti-A or anti-B.
- An ABO-incompatible transfusion causes acute intravascular haemolysis, which can be fatal; this is why bedside identity checks matter.
- Rh D: there are no natural anti-D antibodies. An Rh D-negative person can make IgG anti-D after exposure to Rh D-positive cells, e.g. at delivery. IgG crosses the placenta and can cause haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn in a later Rh D-positive pregnancy. Anti-D immunoglobulin prophylaxis prevents sensitisation.

Exam tips: match test results to pathways (isolated prolonged APTT suggests an intrinsic factor problem), and explain transfusion compatibility by naming the antigens on donor cells and the antibodies in recipient plasma.

The innate immune system responds within minutes to hours, in a similar way each time, using germline-encoded receptors. It also switches on and shapes the adaptive response.

Barriers
Skin, mucous membranes, mucus and cilia in the airways, lysozyme in tears and saliva, gastric acid and the normal microbiota all prevent or limit invasion.

Cells
- Neutrophils: short-lived phagocytes, the main cells of acute inflammation.
- Macrophages: long-lived tissue phagocytes derived from monocytes; release cytokines and present antigen.
- Dendritic cells: capture antigen in tissues, migrate to lymph nodes and activate naive T cells; the key link to adaptive immunity.
- Natural killer (NK) cells: kill virus-infected and tumour cells, particularly those that have lost MHC class I.
- Mast cells: release histamine and other mediators; central to allergic reactions.
- Eosinophils: defence against helminths; involved in allergy and asthma.

Recognition
Pattern recognition receptors, such as the Toll-like receptors, detect pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs), e.g. bacterial lipopolysaccharide sensed by TLR4, and damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) released by injured cells.

Complement
A set of plasma proteins activated by three routes:
- Classical: antibody bound to antigen, recognised by C1q.
- Lectin: mannose-binding lectin binding microbial sugars.
- Alternative: spontaneous C3 activation on unprotected surfaces.
All converge on C3 convertase. Outcomes:
- Opsonisation by C3b, which tags microbes for phagocytosis.
- Inflammation and chemotaxis via the anaphylatoxins C3a and C5a.
- Lysis by the membrane attack complex (C5b–C9). Deficiency of these terminal components predisposes to recurrent Neisseria infection.

Acute inflammation
The classic signs are rubor (redness), calor (heat), tumor (swelling) and dolor (pain), described by Celsus; loss of function (functio laesa) was added later and is often attributed to Virchow.
- Vascular changes: arteriolar dilatation (histamine, prostaglandins, nitric oxide) causes redness and heat; increased venular permeability lets protein-rich exudate escape, causing swelling.
- Cellular events: neutrophils marginate, roll along the endothelium (selectins), adhere firmly (integrins binding ICAM-1), migrate through the vessel wall (diapedesis) and follow chemotactic signals such as C5a, leukotriene B₄ and IL-8 (CXCL8).
- Killing: phagocytosis, then destruction in the phagolysosome by the respiratory burst (NADPH oxidase generating reactive oxygen species) and enzymes. In chronic granulomatous disease, NADPH oxidase is defective and patients get recurrent bacterial and fungal infections.

Systemic effects
IL-1, IL-6 and TNF-α act on the hypothalamus (via prostaglandin E₂) to cause fever, and IL-6 in particular drives the liver to make acute-phase proteins such as C-reactive protein (CRP). Neutrophilia is common in bacterial infection. An excessive, dysregulated systemic response contributes to sepsis.

Outcomes of acute inflammation
- Resolution, if the cause is removed and tissue damage is limited.
- Suppuration and abscess formation.
- Healing by repair and fibrosis (scarring) where tissue cannot regenerate.
- Progression to chronic inflammation, dominated by macrophages, lymphocytes and plasma cells, sometimes forming granulomas (e.g. tuberculosis).

Exam tips: describe acute inflammation as vascular events then cellular events, linking each sign to a mediator, and know the three outcomes of complement activation.

notes.h: Adaptive immunity: B cells, T cells and antibodies
notes.body:
Adaptive immunity is slower to start than innate immunity but is highly specific and has memory. Its key features are specificity, diversity, memory and tolerance of self.

Generating diversity
Each B or T cell expresses a single antigen receptor. The variety of receptors comes from V(D)J recombination of receptor gene segments, carried out by the RAG enzymes, plus random addition of nucleotides at the joins. Developing lymphocytes that react strongly to self are deleted or inactivated (central tolerance in the bone marrow and thymus).

B cells and antibodies
- B cells mature in the bone marrow. Their receptor is membrane-bound immunoglobulin.
- When activated, they become plasma cells that secrete antibody, or memory B cells.
- With help from CD4⁺ T cells (via CD40 ligand binding CD40 and cytokines), B cells switch antibody class and undergo affinity maturation in germinal centres.
Antibody structure: two identical heavy chains and two identical light chains. The Fab regions bind antigen; the Fc region decides what happens next (complement activation, binding to phagocytes or mast cells).
Classes:
- IgM: pentamer, the first antibody in a primary response, strong complement activator.
- IgG: most abundant in serum, crosses the placenta, opsonises and activates complement.
- IgA: dimer in secretions such as saliva, gut mucus and breast milk.
- IgE: binds mast cells and basophils; allergy and anti-parasite defence.
- IgD: mainly a receptor on naive B cells.

T cells
- T cells mature in the thymus. The T-cell receptor recognises a short peptide presented by an MHC molecule (called HLA in humans), not free antigen.
- MHC class I is on all nucleated cells and presents peptides from inside the cell (e.g. viral proteins) to CD8⁺ cytotoxic T cells, which kill the infected cell.
- MHC class II is on professional antigen-presenting cells (dendritic cells, macrophages, B cells) and presents peptides from ingested material to CD4⁺ helper T cells.
- Helper subsets: Th1 (IFN-γ, activates macrophages against intracellular pathogens), Th2 (IL-4, IL-5, IL-13; antibody responses, helminths, allergy), Th17 (neutrophil recruitment, extracellular bacteria and fungi), regulatory T cells (express FOXP3, suppress responses and maintain tolerance).

Two-signal activation
A naive T cell needs signal 1 (TCR binding peptide–MHC) and signal 2 (co-stimulation, e.g. CD28 binding CD80/CD86 on an activated antigen-presenting cell). Signal 1 without signal 2 tends to cause anergy, a safeguard against responding to self.

Primary and secondary responses
The first exposure gives a slow response over days, dominated early by IgM. A second exposure triggers memory cells, producing a faster, larger response that is mainly IgG with higher affinity. This is the basis of vaccination.
- Active immunity: the body makes its own response (infection, vaccination); long-lasting.
- Passive immunity: antibodies are transferred (maternal IgG across the placenta, IgA in breast milk, immunoglobulin products); immediate but temporary.

Hypersensitivity (Gell and Coombs classification)
- Type I: IgE-mediated, immediate (hay fever, anaphylaxis).
- Type II: antibody against antigens on cells or tissues (ABO-incompatible transfusion reaction, Goodpasture syndrome).
- Type III: immune-complex deposition (systemic lupus erythematosus, post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis).
- Type IV: T-cell mediated, delayed by 48–72 hours (contact dermatitis, tuberculin skin test).

Clinical link
HIV infects CD4⁺ T cells; their progressive loss weakens both cell-mediated and antibody responses and leads to opportunistic infections.

Exam tips: pair each MHC class with its source of antigen and its T-cell partner, and use a labelled graph of antibody level against time to explain primary versus secondary responses.

notes.h: Genetics: DNA, gene expression and inheritance
notes.body:
Genetics links molecular biology to patterns of disease in families and populations.

DNA and replication
- DNA is a double helix of two antiparallel strands (structure described by Watson and Crick in 1953). Adenine pairs with thymine (two hydrogen bonds) and guanine with cytosine (three).
- Replication is semi-conservative: each new molecule has one old and one new strand, shown by Meselson and Stahl (1958).
- DNA polymerase only adds nucleotides in the 5'→3' direction, so one strand is made continuously (leading) and the other in Okazaki fragments (lagging), later joined by DNA ligase.

From gene to protein
- Transcription in the nucleus: RNA polymerase II makes pre-mRNA from the template strand.
- Processing: a 5' cap and 3' poly-A tail are added and introns are removed by splicing. Alternative splicing lets one gene make several proteins.
- Translation on ribosomes: each three-base codon specifies an amino acid, carried by tRNA. AUG (methionine) is the usual start codon; UAA, UAG and UGA are stop codons. The code is degenerate: most amino acids have more than one codon.

Mutations
- Silent: a base change that does not alter the amino acid.
- Missense: changes one amino acid. Sickle cell disease results from glutamate being replaced by valine at position 6 of β-globin.
- Nonsense: creates a premature stop codon.
- Frameshift: insertion or deletion of bases not in a multiple of three, scrambling everything downstream. The commonest cystic fibrosis variant, F508del, deletes three bases, so it removes one phenylalanine without a frameshift.
- Repeat expansions: Huntington disease is caused by an expanded CAG repeat in HTT; longer repeats tend to give earlier onset, and repeats can expand between generations (anticipation).

Patterns of inheritance
- Autosomal dominant: one altered copy is enough; affected parent has a 1 in 2 chance of passing it on to each child; usually seen in every generation, although reduced penetrance or a new mutation can break this pattern (e.g. Huntington disease, familial hypercholesterolaemia).
- Autosomal recessive: two altered copies needed; parents are usually unaffected carriers (e.g. cystic fibrosis, sickle cell disease).
- X-linked recessive: mainly affects males, who have one X; no male-to-male transmission (e.g. haemophilia A, Duchenne muscular dystrophy).
- Mitochondrial: passed only from the mother, with variable severity because cells contain mixtures of normal and altered mitochondria (heteroplasmy).

Worked example: two carrier parents (Aa × Aa)
Offspring: 1/4 AA, 1/2 Aa, 1/4 aa. So each child has a 1 in 4 chance of being affected. If a child is known to be unaffected, the chance that they are a carrier is 2/3 (two carrier outcomes out of three unaffected outcomes).

Hardy–Weinberg
In a large, randomly mating population with no selection, migration or new mutation, p² + 2pq + q² = 1, where p and q are allele frequencies. Illustrative example: if a recessive condition affects 1 in 2,500 births, q² = 1/2,500, so q = 0.02 and p = 0.98. Carrier frequency 2pq = 2 × 0.98 × 0.02 ≈ 0.039, about 1 in 25. A common error is to forget the factor of 2 or to use q instead of 2pq.

Chromosomes and meiosis
Meiosis halves the chromosome number and creates variation through crossing over (prophase I) and independent assortment. Non-disjunction gives aneuploidy: trisomy 21 (Down syndrome), whose risk rises with maternal age; 45,X (Turner syndrome); 47,XXY (Klinefelter syndrome).

Exam tips: draw a Punnett square or pedigree, state the mode of inheritance with evidence from the pedigree (e.g. male-to-male transmission excludes X-linked inheritance), and show each Hardy–Weinberg step.

cards.b: Membrane as a phospholipid bilayer with proteins embedded in or attached to it, free to move laterally; proposed by Singer and Nicolson in 1972.
Per ATP hydrolysed it pumps 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ into the cell; it is electrogenic and maintains the Na⁺ gradient used for secondary active transport.
Moving a solute against its gradient using energy stored in another ion's gradient (usually Na⁺), e.g. SGLT1 co-transporting Na⁺ and glucose.
Rate of diffusion ∝ surface area × concentration difference ÷ thickness of the barrier.

9 g/L ÷ 58.44 g/mol ≈ 154 mmol/L; two particles per NaCl gives a theoretical 308 mOsm/L. Non-ideal behaviour lowers the effective value to about 285 mOsm/kg, close to plasma, so it is roughly isotonic.
Acidic organelles (pH about 4.5–5) containing hydrolytic enzymes that digest engulfed and worn-out material.
Cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator: an epithelial chloride channel; faulty in cystic fibrosis, giving thick secretions.
The substrate concentration at which the reaction rate is half of Vmax.
v = Vmax[S] / (Km + [S])

cards.f: Competitive inhibition: effect on Km and Vmax
cards.b: Apparent Km increases; Vmax unchanged; overcome by raising substrate concentration.

cards.f: Non-competitive inhibition: effect on Km and Vmax
cards.b: Vmax decreases; Km unchanged; extra substrate cannot overcome it.
y-intercept = 1/Vmax; x-intercept = −1/Km; slope = Km/Vmax.
Glucokinase (liver, β cells): high Km, not inhibited by glucose-6-phosphate, acts as glucose sensor. Hexokinase: low Km, product-inhibited.

cards.f: Do enzymes change the equilibrium of a reaction?
cards.b: No. They lower the activation energy so equilibrium is reached faster; ΔG and the equilibrium position are unchanged.

cards.f: Net yield of glycolysis per glucose
cards.b: 2 ATP (net) and 2 NADH, plus 2 pyruvate.
Phosphofructokinase-1: activated by AMP and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate; inhibited by ATP and citrate.

cards.f: Products of one turn of the TCA cycle
cards.b: 3 NADH, 1 FADH₂, 1 GTP (or ATP) and 2 CO₂.
They lack mitochondria, so they depend on glycolysis; lactate dehydrogenase regenerates NAD⁺ to keep glycolysis running.
Mitchell (1961): electron transport pumps protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane; ATP synthase uses the proton gradient to make ATP.
Inhibits complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase), blocking transfer of electrons to oxygen.
Thermogenin in brown fat: lets protons leak back into the matrix without making ATP, releasing energy as heat.
Glucose → GLUT2 → glucokinase → ↑ATP → K-ATP channels close → depolarisation → Ca²⁺ influx → insulin exocytosis.
Insulin-responsive glucose transporter in skeletal muscle and adipose tissue; insulin moves it to the cell surface.

cards.f: Why muscle glycogen cannot raise blood glucose
cards.b: Muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase, so glucose-6-phosphate cannot be released as free glucose.
Lactate (Cori cycle), alanine and other glucogenic amino acids, and glycerol from triglyceride.

cards.f: Why even-chain fatty acids cannot make net glucose
cards.b: They yield acetyl-CoA, and the pyruvate dehydrogenase reaction is irreversible, so acetyl-CoA cannot become pyruvate.
Acetoacetate and β-hydroxybutyrate (acetone is a by-product), made by the liver in prolonged fasting or insulin deficiency.
Average glycaemia over about the previous 2–3 months, because red cells live about 120 days.
Peritubular interstitial cells of the kidney, responding to low oxygen delivery.
About 120 days; old cells are removed by macrophages, mainly in the spleen.

cards.f: Factors shifting the O₂ dissociation curve right
cards.b: Raised CO₂, raised H⁺ (Bohr effect), raised temperature, raised 2,3-BPG: Hb gives up O₂ more readily.

cards.f: Why HbF has higher O₂ affinity
cards.b: HbF (α₂γ₂) binds 2,3-BPG poorly, so its dissociation curve is shifted left.
Liver hormone that blocks ferroportin, reducing iron absorption and release from stores; rises in inflammation.
B12 or folate deficiency, alcohol excess, liver disease, hypothyroidism, reticulocytosis.
Terminal ileum, bound to intrinsic factor from gastric parietal cells.
Bridges exposed collagen to platelet glycoprotein Ib (adhesion) and carries factor VIII in plasma.
II, VII, IX and X, plus the anticoagulant proteins C and S.
PT/INR: extrinsic + common pathways. APTT: intrinsic + common pathways.
Stasis of blood flow, endothelial injury and hypercoagulability.
X-linked recessive deficiency of factor VIII; prolonged APTT, normal PT; joint and muscle bleeding.
Anti-A and anti-B (mainly IgM, naturally occurring).

cards.f: Haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn (anti-D)
cards.b: Rh D-negative mother sensitised to Rh D makes IgG anti-D, which crosses the placenta and destroys Rh D-positive fetal red cells.
Pathogen-associated molecular patterns (e.g. LPS) are detected by pattern recognition receptors such as Toll-like receptors (LPS via TLR4).
Opsonisation (C3b), inflammation/chemotaxis (C3a, C5a) and lysis by the membrane attack complex (C5b–C9).
Rubor, calor, tumor, dolor (Celsus); functio laesa added later.
Margination, rolling (selectins), firm adhesion (integrins–ICAM-1), transmigration, chemotaxis.
Defective NADPH oxidase, so phagocytes cannot make a respiratory burst; recurrent bacterial and fungal infections.
IL-6, acting on hepatocytes.
CD8⁺ cytotoxic T cells; found on all nucleated cells; presents peptides from inside the cell.
CD4⁺ helper T cells; found on antigen-presenting cells; presents peptides from ingested material.
IgG.

cards.f: First antibody of a primary response
cards.b: IgM (pentameric, strong complement activator).
Co-stimulation, e.g. CD28 on the T cell binding CD80/CD86 on the antigen-presenting cell; without it, anergy.
Delayed (48–72 h), T-cell mediated; e.g. contact dermatitis, tuberculin skin test.
CD4⁺ T cells expressing FOXP3 that suppress immune responses and maintain tolerance.
Each daughter DNA molecule has one parental and one new strand (Meselson and Stahl, 1958).
UAA, UAG and UGA.
Missense: glutamate → valine at position 6 of β-globin.
Insertion or deletion of bases not in a multiple of three, altering the reading frame downstream.

cards.f: Carrier probability of an unaffected child of two carriers

cards.b: 2pq; for a recessive disease with incidence 1 in 2,500, q = 0.02 and 2pq ≈ 1 in 25.
Male-to-male transmission (fathers pass a Y, not an X, to sons).
Earlier onset or greater severity in successive generations, typically from repeat expansion (e.g. Huntington disease).

questions.q: Which transport process moves glucose into intestinal epithelial cells against its concentration gradient?
options: Simple diffusion through the lipid bilayer
Primary active transport by a glucose-ATPase
questions.why: SGLT1 couples glucose entry to Na⁺ moving down the gradient that the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase creates, so it can move glucose uphill: that is secondary active transport. Simple diffusion is wrong because glucose is polar and does not cross the bilayer unaided, and diffusion can only go downhill. GLUT2 facilitated diffusion is a real step, but it lets glucose leave the cell on the blood side, down its gradient. There is no glucose-pumping ATPase; the ATP is spent by the Na⁺/K⁺ pump, not by the glucose carrier itself.

questions.q: Approximately what is the theoretical osmolarity of 0.9% sodium chloride solution (molar mass 58.44 g/mol)?
questions.why: 0.9% means 9 g/L; 9 ÷ 58.44 ≈ 0.154 mol/L = 154 mmol/L, and each NaCl gives two particles, so about 308 mOsm/L. The 154 mOsm/L answer is the molarity, forgetting that NaCl dissociates into Na⁺ and Cl⁻. The 9 mOsm/L answer treats grams per litre as if it were osmoles. The 15.4 mOsm/L answer comes from reading 0.9% as 0.9 g/L instead of 9 g/L (0.9 g per 100 mL) and also ignoring dissociation.

questions.q: Explain how the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase allows the small intestine to absorb glucose, and why oral rehydration solution contains both sodium and glucose.
markScheme: Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase on the basolateral membrane pumps 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in per ATP, keeping intracellular Na⁺ low
This creates an inward Na⁺ electrochemical gradient across the apical membrane
SGLT1 co-transports Na⁺ and glucose into the enterocyte (secondary active transport), moving glucose against its gradient
Glucose leaves across the basolateral membrane by facilitated diffusion (GLUT2)
In ORS, glucose-coupled Na⁺ uptake still works in many diarrhoeal illnesses; absorbed solute draws water osmotically
questions.modelAnswer: The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase on the basolateral side of the enterocyte uses ATP to pump three Na⁺ out and two K⁺ in, keeping intracellular Na⁺ low. This sets up a steep inward Na⁺ gradient across the apical membrane. SGLT1 uses that gradient to carry Na⁺ and glucose into the cell together, so glucose can be taken up even when its concentration inside the cell is higher than in the lumen: this is secondary active transport. Glucose then leaves the cell into the blood by facilitated diffusion through GLUT2. Oral rehydration solution exploits this: in many diarrhoeal illnesses SGLT1 still works, so supplying sodium together with glucose drives solute absorption, and water follows osmotically, replacing lost fluid.

questions.q: An enzyme has Vmax = 100 units and Km = 2 mM. What is the rate at a substrate concentration of 6 mM?
questions.why: v = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]) = 100 × 6 / (2 + 6) = 75. The 50-unit answer is the rate when [S] equals Km, so it ignores the higher substrate concentration. The 300-unit answer multiplies Vmax by [S]/Km, forgetting the Km + [S] denominator and allowing a rate above Vmax, which is impossible. The 25-unit answer uses Km/(Km + [S]) instead of [S]/(Km + [S]), i.e. the fraction of enzyme unoccupied.

questions.q: Which pattern on kinetic analysis indicates a competitive inhibitor?
questions.why: A competitive inhibitor occupies the active site, so more substrate is needed to reach half Vmax (apparent Km rises), but at very high substrate the inhibitor is outcompeted and Vmax is still reached. A fall in Vmax with Km unchanged describes non-competitive inhibition, where the inhibitor binds elsewhere. Both falling describes uncompetitive inhibition, where the inhibitor binds only the enzyme–substrate complex. No inhibitor raises Vmax; that pattern would suggest an activator.

questions.q: Compare hexokinase and glucokinase and explain why the difference matters after a carbohydrate-rich meal.
markScheme: Both phosphorylate glucose to glucose-6-phosphate
Hexokinase: most tissues, low Km, inhibited by glucose-6-phosphate
Glucokinase: liver and pancreatic β cells, much higher Km, not inhibited by glucose-6-phosphate
After a meal glucokinase activity rises with portal glucose, so the liver can take up and store large amounts, and β cells sense glucose to release insulin
questions.modelAnswer: Both enzymes phosphorylate glucose to glucose-6-phosphate, trapping it in the cell. Hexokinase, found in most tissues, has a low Km, so it works near maximum rate even at fasting glucose levels, and it is inhibited by its product, glucose-6-phosphate, so tissues take only what they need. Glucokinase, in the liver and pancreatic β cells, has a much higher Km and is not product-inhibited. Its activity therefore keeps rising as glucose rises. After a carbohydrate-rich meal, portal glucose is high, so hepatic glucokinase lets the liver take up large amounts for glycogen storage, and in β cells it links glucose concentration to ATP production and insulin release, acting as a glucose sensor.

questions.q: Where does the pyruvate dehydrogenase reaction take place?
questions.why: Pyruvate is transported into mitochondria and converted to acetyl-CoA by the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex in the matrix, where the TCA cycle also runs. The cytosol is where glycolysis makes pyruvate, so choosing it confuses the producing pathway with the next step. The intermembrane space is where protons accumulate during electron transport, not a site of fuel oxidation. The smooth ER handles lipid synthesis and detoxification, not pyruvate oxidation.

questions.q: Using about 2.5 ATP per NADH and 1.5 per FADH₂, and assuming cytosolic NADH is fully used via the malate–aspartate shuttle, roughly how much ATP is made from complete oxidation of one glucose?
questions.why: 10 NADH × 2.5 = 25, 2 FADH₂ × 1.5 = 3, plus 4 ATP/GTP made directly = 32. About 38 is the older textbook figure that used whole-number ratios of 3 per NADH and 2 per FADH₂. About 2 is just the net yield of glycolysis alone, as in anaerobic conditions. About 7 counts glycolysis only (2 ATP plus 2 NADH × 2.5 = 7), forgetting that the two pyruvates are then oxidised in the mitochondria, where most of the ATP is made.

questions.q: Explain why cyanide poisoning causes a lactic acidosis.
markScheme: Cyanide inhibits complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase)
Electron transfer to O₂ stops, so the proton gradient and oxidative phosphorylation fail
NADH cannot be reoxidised by the chain, so the NADH/NAD⁺ ratio rises and the TCA cycle slows
Cells rely on anaerobic glycolysis; pyruvate is reduced to lactate by LDH to regenerate NAD⁺
Lactate (with H⁺) accumulates, causing a metabolic (lactic) acidosis even though blood O₂ may be normal
questions.modelAnswer: Cyanide binds and inhibits complex IV, cytochrome c oxidase, which passes electrons to oxygen. Electron transport therefore stops, protons are no longer pumped and ATP synthase cannot make ATP by oxidative phosphorylation. NADH can no longer be reoxidised by the chain, so NAD⁺ runs short and the TCA cycle and pyruvate dehydrogenase slow. Cells fall back on glycolysis, which can continue only if NAD⁺ is regenerated, and this is done by lactate dehydrogenase reducing pyruvate to lactate. Lactate and hydrogen ions accumulate, producing a lactic acidosis. Oxygen delivery may be normal, but tissues cannot use it.

questions.q: Why can skeletal muscle glycogen not be used to maintain blood glucose during fasting?
options: Muscle cells have no GLUT transporters
Muscle glycogen is converted directly into fatty acids
questions.why: Muscle breaks down glycogen to glucose-6-phosphate but lacks glucose-6-phosphatase, so it cannot release free glucose; it uses the glucose-6-phosphate itself. Muscle does have glycogen phosphorylase, which is why it can mobilise glycogen during exercise. Muscle has GLUT4 (and GLUT1), so lack of transporters is false. Glycogen is not converted into fatty acids in muscle; this confuses storage pathways with the actual block at the final step.

questions.q: During prolonged starvation, which change most reduces the breakdown of muscle protein?
options: The brain using ketone bodies for much of its fuel
Conversion of fatty acids into glucose
questions.why: In prolonged starvation the brain adapts to use ketone bodies, so less glucose has to be made by gluconeogenesis from amino acids, sparing muscle protein. Insulin falls, not rises, during starvation. Even-chain fatty acids cannot be turned into net glucose because the pyruvate dehydrogenase step is irreversible, so that option relies on a common misconception. Liver glycogen is largely used up within about a day of fasting, so it is not increasing.

questions.q: Describe how insulin release from pancreatic β cells is coupled to blood glucose concentration.
markScheme: Glucose enters β cells via GLUT2
Glucokinase phosphorylates it; metabolism raises ATP/ADP ratio
ATP-sensitive K⁺ channels close
Membrane depolarises, opening voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels
Ca²⁺ influx triggers exocytosis of insulin granules
questions.modelAnswer: Glucose enters the β cell through GLUT2 in proportion to the blood concentration and is phosphorylated by glucokinase, which, having a high Km, works as the glucose sensor. Glycolysis and oxidative metabolism raise the ATP/ADP ratio. ATP closes ATP-sensitive K⁺ channels, so less K⁺ leaves and the membrane depolarises. Depolarisation opens voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels; the resulting Ca²⁺ influx triggers exocytosis of insulin-containing granules. The higher the glucose, the greater the ATP rise and the more insulin is secreted.

questions.q: Which change shifts the haemoglobin–oxygen dissociation curve to the left?
questions.why: HbF binds 2,3-BPG poorly, so it holds O₂ more tightly and its curve lies to the left; this helps the fetus take O₂ from maternal blood. Raised 2,3-BPG, raised temperature and a fall in pH (more H⁺, the Bohr effect) all shift the curve to the right, increasing O₂ unloading. Choosing any of these reverses the direction of the shift.

questions.q: A patient has a low haemoglobin, a low MCV and a low ferritin. What is the most likely cause?
questions.why: Microcytic anaemia with low ferritin indicates depleted iron stores, i.e. iron deficiency. B12 deficiency gives a macrocytic, not microcytic, picture. Anaemia of chronic disease can be microcytic, but ferritin is usually normal or raised because it is an acute-phase protein and iron is trapped in stores. Acute haemolysis is typically normocytic (or slightly macrocytic from reticulocytes) and does not lower ferritin.

questions.q: Explain why chronic kidney disease commonly causes a normocytic anaemia.
markScheme: Erythropoietin is made mainly by peritubular interstitial cells of the kidney
Damaged kidneys make less EPO relative to the degree of anaemia
Less EPO means less stimulation of red cell precursors in marrow, so production falls
Cells made are of normal size (normocytic); other contributors include reduced iron availability and shorter red cell survival
questions.modelAnswer: Erythropoietin, the hormone that drives red cell production, is produced mainly by peritubular interstitial cells in the kidney in response to low oxygen delivery. In chronic kidney disease these cells are lost or impaired, so EPO output is inappropriately low for the degree of anaemia. With less EPO, the marrow makes fewer red cells, but the cells it does make are of normal size, giving a normocytic anaemia. Other factors add to it, such as reduced iron availability linked to inflammation (raised hepcidin) and shortened red cell survival.

questions.q: A boy has a prolonged APTT, a normal PT and recurrent bleeding into his knees. Which deficiency is most likely?
questions.why: An isolated prolonged APTT points to the intrinsic pathway, and haemarthroses in a boy suggest haemophilia A (factor VIII deficiency, X-linked). Factor VII deficiency would prolong the PT, because VII is in the extrinsic pathway. Vitamin K deficiency reduces II, VII, IX and X, so it would prolong the PT (and usually the APTT). Low platelets cause mucosal and skin bleeding (petechiae) rather than joint bleeds, and do not prolong the APTT.

questions.q: A patient with blood group A needs red cells urgently. Which donor red cells are ABO-compatible?
questions.why: A group A recipient has anti-B in their plasma, so donor red cells must not carry B antigen: group A and group O cells are compatible. Group B cells carry B antigen and would be haemolysed. Group AB cells also carry B antigen, so both answers that include AB are wrong; that error comes from applying plasma compatibility rules (where AB is the universal donor) to red cells.

questions.q: Outline the steps in forming a primary platelet plug and explain how aspirin affects it.
markScheme: Vessel injury exposes subendothelial collagen; brief vasoconstriction
Adhesion: vWF links collagen to platelet GPIb
Activation: shape change and release of ADP and thromboxane A₂ recruit more platelets
Aggregation: GPIIb/IIIa binds fibrinogen, cross-linking platelets
Aspirin irreversibly acetylates COX, blocking TXA₂ production for the platelet's lifespan (platelets lack nuclei to make new enzyme)
questions.modelAnswer: When a vessel is injured it constricts briefly, and subendothelial collagen is exposed. Von Willebrand factor binds the collagen and captures platelets through glycoprotein Ib (adhesion). Adherent platelets are activated: they change shape and release ADP and thromboxane A₂, which recruit and activate more platelets. Activated glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptors then bind fibrinogen, linking platelets into a plug (aggregation). Aspirin irreversibly acetylates cyclo-oxygenase, so platelets cannot make thromboxane A₂. Because platelets lack a nucleus they cannot make new enzyme, so the effect lasts for the rest of their lifespan of about 7–10 days.

questions.q: Which complement fragment acts mainly as an opsonin?
questions.why: C3b coats microbes and is recognised by receptors on phagocytes, promoting phagocytosis (opsonisation). C3a and C5a are small anaphylatoxins that cause inflammation and attract cells; choosing them mixes up the 'a' and 'b' fragments. C5b–C9 is the membrane attack complex, which lyses cells rather than tagging them.

questions.q: In acute inflammation, what mainly causes the swelling?
options: Proliferation of fibroblasts at the site
Increased vascular permeability allowing protein-rich exudate into tissues
Arteriolar constriction trapping blood in capillaries
questions.why: Mediators such as histamine increase the permeability of venules, so protein-rich fluid leaks into the tissue (exudate), causing swelling. Fibroblast proliferation is a feature of repair and fibrosis, which comes later. Inflammation causes arteriolar dilatation, not constriction; dilatation explains redness and heat. Lymphocyte infiltration is typical of chronic, not acute, inflammation, where neutrophils dominate.

questions.q: Describe the sequence of events by which neutrophils leave the blood and reach bacteria in an inflamed tissue.
markScheme: Margination: slowed flow from vasodilatation pushes neutrophils to the vessel wall
Rolling: selectins on activated endothelium bind neutrophil ligands
Firm adhesion: integrins (activated by chemokines) bind ICAM-1
Transmigration (diapedesis) between endothelial cells through the basement membrane
Chemotaxis towards C5a, LTB₄, IL-8; then phagocytosis and killing
questions.modelAnswer: Vasodilatation slows blood flow, so neutrophils move to the edge of the stream (margination). Activated endothelium expresses selectins, which bind neutrophil surface ligands loosely, making the cells roll along the wall. Chemokines activate neutrophil integrins, which bind ICAM-1 firmly, stopping the cells. Neutrophils then squeeze between endothelial cells and cross the basement membrane (transmigration or diapedesis). In the tissue they follow gradients of chemotactic agents such as C5a, leukotriene B₄ and IL-8 to the bacteria, which they phagocytose and kill using the respiratory burst and enzymes.

questions.q: A virus-infected epithelial cell is recognised and killed by a cytotoxic T cell. Which molecule presents the viral peptide?
questions.why: Peptides from proteins made inside a cell, such as viral proteins, are presented on MHC class I, which is found on all nucleated cells and recognised by CD8⁺ cytotoxic T cells. MHC class II presents ingested antigen on antigen-presenting cells to CD4⁺ helper cells, and ordinary epithelial cells do not normally express much of it. CD4 is a co-receptor on helper T cells, not a presenting molecule. Membrane IgM is the B-cell receptor, which binds intact antigen, not peptide presented to T cells.

questions.q: Contact dermatitis to nickel appearing 48 hours after exposure is which type of hypersensitivity?
questions.why: A reaction delayed by about two days and mediated by sensitised T cells is type IV (delayed-type) hypersensitivity. Type I is IgE-mediated and occurs within minutes. Type II involves antibody against cell-surface antigens (e.g. transfusion reactions). Type III involves immune complexes deposited in vessels or tissues. Choosing an antibody-mediated type ignores the delay, which points to T cells.

questions.q: Explain why the antibody response to a second exposure to the same antigen differs from the first.
markScheme: Primary response: lag of days; low-affinity antibody, mainly IgM early
Memory B and T cells form after the primary response
Secondary response: shorter lag, higher peak, longer-lasting
Mainly IgG (class switching) with higher affinity (affinity maturation in germinal centres)
Basis of vaccination / booster doses
questions.modelAnswer: On first exposure, naive lymphocytes specific for the antigen are rare and must be activated, so there is a lag of several days; the early antibody is mainly IgM and of relatively low affinity. During this response, T-cell help drives class switching and affinity maturation in germinal centres, and long-lived memory B and T cells form. On a second exposure, these more numerous memory cells respond quickly, so the lag is shorter, the antibody peak is much higher and lasts longer, and the antibody is mostly IgG of higher affinity. Vaccination uses this principle, and booster doses exploit the secondary response.

questions.q: Two unaffected parents each carry one copy of a recessive cystic fibrosis variant. Their first child is unaffected. What is the probability that this child is a carrier?
questions.why: The possible genotypes are 1/4 AA, 1/2 Aa, 1/4 aa. Knowing the child is unaffected removes aa, leaving three equally likely outcomes, two of which are carriers: 2/3. The 1/2 answer is the carrier probability before we know the child is unaffected. The 1/4 answer is the chance of being affected. The 3/4 answer is the chance of being unaffected, not of being a carrier.

questions.q: A recessive disorder affects 1 in 2,500 births in a population in Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium. What is the approximate carrier frequency?
questions.why: q² = 1/2,500, so q = 0.02 and p = 0.98. Carrier frequency 2pq = 2 × 0.98 × 0.02 ≈ 0.039, about 1 in 25. The 1 in 50 answer is q itself (the allele frequency), forgetting that carriers are 2pq. The 1 in 2,500 answer is the disease frequency q². The 1 in 1,250 answer doubles the disease frequency (2q² = 2/2,500), applying the factor of 2 to q² instead of to pq, as if carriers were simply twice as common as affected people.

questions.q: Using a pedigree, how would you distinguish autosomal dominant from X-linked recessive inheritance? Give an example of each.
markScheme: Autosomal dominant: affected individuals in every generation; each child of an affected parent has 1 in 2 risk
Males and females affected equally; male-to-male transmission occurs
X-linked recessive: mainly males affected, often skipping generations via carrier females
No male-to-male transmission; affected male's daughters are all carriers
Examples: Huntington disease or familial hypercholesterolaemia (AD); haemophilia A or Duchenne (XLR)
questions.modelAnswer: In autosomal dominant inheritance, one altered copy causes disease, so affected people usually appear in every generation, each child of an affected parent has a 1 in 2 chance of inheriting it, both sexes are affected equally and father-to-son transmission can occur. Huntington disease and familial hypercholesterolaemia are examples. In X-linked recessive inheritance, males (with a single X) are mainly affected; the condition often seems to skip generations because it passes through unaffected carrier females; there is never male-to-male transmission, because fathers give sons a Y chromosome; and all daughters of an affected man are carriers. Haemophilia A and Duchenne muscular dystrophy are examples. Seeing father-to-son transmission therefore rules out X-linked inheritance.

questions.q: A previously healthy adult fasts for three days, drinking only water. Describe how fuel use changes across this period and explain how hormones coordinate these changes. Use the liver, skeletal muscle, adipose tissue and brain in your answer.
markScheme: Fed-to-fasting switch: falling insulin, rising glucagon (plus adrenaline, cortisol, GH)
Early fast: hepatic glycogenolysis maintains glucose; liver glycogen largely depleted within about a day
Gluconeogenesis in liver from lactate (Cori cycle), alanine and glycerol; muscle protein breakdown supplies amino acids
Adipose lipolysis (low insulin removes inhibition) releases fatty acids used by muscle and liver; even-chain fatty acids cannot make net glucose
Hepatic ketogenesis from acetyl-CoA; ketones used increasingly by brain, sparing protein
Red cells remain glucose-dependent (no mitochondria); muscle glycogen cannot supply blood glucose (no glucose-6-phosphatase)
Clear, tissue-by-tissue and time-ordered structure
questions.modelAnswer:
During the first hours after the last meal, absorbed glucose is used and stored while insulin is high. As glucose falls, insulin secretion falls and glucagon rises; adrenaline, cortisol and growth hormone add to the counter-regulatory response. The low insulin to glucagon ratio is the key signal.

Liver. Early in the fast, glucagon activates hepatic glycogenolysis, releasing glucose into the blood. Liver glycogen is largely used up within roughly a day, so gluconeogenesis becomes the main source of glucose. Substrates are lactate returned from red cells and muscle (the Cori cycle), alanine and other glucogenic amino acids from muscle protein, and glycerol from triglyceride breakdown. As the fast continues, the liver oxidises fatty acids and, because acetyl-CoA exceeds what the TCA cycle can handle, converts it into ketone bodies (acetoacetate and β-hydroxybutyrate), which are exported.

Adipose tissue. Low insulin removes the brake on lipolysis, and catecholamines (adrenaline and sympathetic noradrenaline) promote it. Triglyceride is broken down into fatty acids, which travel bound to albumin, and glycerol, which goes to the liver for gluconeogenesis. Even-chain fatty acids cannot make net glucose because the pyruvate dehydrogenase reaction is irreversible.

Skeletal muscle. Resting muscle switches to fatty acids and, later, ketones. Its glycogen is used only locally, because muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase. Muscle protein is broken down to provide amino acids for gluconeogenesis; cortisol encourages this.

Brain. The brain cannot use fatty acids directly and relies on glucose at first. As ketone concentrations rise over several days, it uses ketones for a growing share of its energy. This reduces the demand for glucose and therefore for gluconeogenesis from amino acids, sparing muscle protein. Red blood cells, lacking mitochondria, remain dependent on glucose throughout.

By day three, then, blood glucose is kept within a near-normal range mainly by hepatic gluconeogenesis, most tissues run on fatty acids and ketones, and the hormonal pattern of low insulin and high glucagon coordinates the switch.

questions.q: A child receives a vaccine against a bacterial toxin. Explain the innate and adaptive immune events that lead to long-term protection, and explain why a later booster produces a stronger response than the first dose.
markScheme: Innate recognition (often helped by adjuvant) activates dendritic cells via PRRs; antigen uptake and migration to lymph node
Antigen presentation on MHC class II to naive CD4⁺ T cells with co-stimulation (signal 1 + signal 2)
B cells binding toxin via BCR internalise and present it; T-cell help (CD40L–CD40, cytokines) activates them
Germinal centre reactions: class switching to IgG and affinity maturation; plasma cells secrete antibody
Memory B and T cells and long-lived plasma cells give lasting protection; neutralising IgG blocks toxin
Booster triggers memory cells: shorter lag, higher, longer-lasting, higher-affinity IgG (secondary response)
Accurate terminology and logical sequence
questions.modelAnswer:
A toxin vaccine usually contains an inactivated form of the toxin (a toxoid), often with an adjuvant. At the injection site, the adjuvant and tissue damage stimulate innate cells through pattern recognition receptors. Dendritic cells take up the antigen, become activated, raise co-stimulatory molecules such as CD80/CD86, and migrate to the draining lymph node.

In the lymph node, dendritic cells present peptides from the toxoid on MHC class II to naive CD4⁺ helper T cells. A T cell whose receptor recognises the peptide–MHC complex (signal 1) and also receives co-stimulation through CD28 (signal 2) becomes activated and proliferates. Without signal 2 it would tend to become anergic, which is one reason adjuvants matter.

Meanwhile, B cells whose receptors bind the intact toxoid internalise it and present its peptides on their own MHC class II. Activated helper T cells recognise these B cells and provide help through CD40 ligand binding CD40 and through cytokines. The B cells proliferate; some become plasma cells secreting IgM early in the response, while others enter germinal centres. There, class switching produces IgG, and affinity maturation selects B cells with higher-affinity receptors.

The result is a pool of plasma cells making neutralising IgG, which binds the toxin and stops it attaching to its target cells, together with long-lived plasma cells and memory B and T cells. These provide lasting protection.

The first dose produces a primary response: a lag of days, a modest peak and early IgM. A booster acts on the expanded memory population. Because memory cells are more numerous and more easily activated, the secondary response has a shorter lag, a much higher and more sustained antibody level, and is dominated by high-affinity IgG. Each booster can drive further affinity maturation and refresh memory, which is why schedules often include more than one dose.
